opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the genuinely open questions, and I'd put real but not overwhelming probability on it. Coding, math, anything where you can check whether the answer is right: those are where reinforcement learning works most cleanly, because you have a reward signal you can trust. So it's natural to ask whether we'll end up with models that are superhuman at proving theorems and writing software but still mediocre at the fuzzier things, like judgment, taste, or knowing which problem is worth working on in the first place.

My sense is that it's less of a cliff than people imagine, for a few reasons. First, what we've seen empirically is a lot of generalization. When you train models on verifiable tasks, they don't just get better at those tasks. They get better at reasoning in general, at being careful, at checking their own work. Those habits transfer. It's not perfect transfer, but it's not zero either.

Second, a lot of things that look unverifiable are more verifiable than they seem once you decompose them. Writing a good scientific paper isn't verifiable as a whole, but many pieces of it are: does the experiment replicate, does the code run, does the statistic hold up. And you can use models themselves as graders for the softer parts, which has its own problems but works better than you'd naively expect.

Third, even in the pessimistic scenario, the verifiable domains are enormously consequential. If you get to the point where AI can do most of software engineering and much of the mathematical and computational side of science, that by itself is a huge acceleration, including of AI research itself. That can then help close the gap on the harder-to-verify stuff.

That said, I don't want to dismiss the concern. I can imagine a world where we hit something like a jagged frontier that stays jagged for longer than I'd expect, where models are brilliant at closed-form problems and still need humans for open-ended direction. If that happens, the timelines I talk about would stretch out, and the economic picture would look more like strong complementarity than substitution for a while. I just don't think that's the most likely outcome, given the trends we've seen so far. But it's one of the things I watch most closely.

r001.rationale: The candidate says transfer from verifiable tasks to broader reasoning is “not perfect” but “not zero,” and describes the gap as less of a cliff than an all-or-nothing divide.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I take that possibility seriously, and I think it's one of the real live uncertainties about how the next couple of years go. The way I'd frame it is: the thing that's clearly working right now is RL on tasks where you can check the answer. Math, code, anything where there's a compiler or a test or a proof checker at the end. And the question is whether what you learn there transfers to the things that don't have that structure. Writing a good essay. Running a negotiation. Figuring out what a customer actually wants when they've described it badly. Doing science where the experiment takes six months to come back.

My honest view is that I don't think it falls short, but I want to be careful about why I think that, because I could be wrong.

The first reason is that we've already seen a surprising amount of transfer. When you train a model hard on math and code, it tends to get better at reasoning in general, at breaking problems into steps, at noticing when it's made a mistake. Those are not domain-specific skills. The model is learning something more like "how to think carefully," and that shows up in places you didn't train for. That's been a consistent surprise in the positive direction.

The second reason is that the boundary of "verifiable" is a lot softer than people assume. People treat it as a hard line, but a lot of what looks unverifiable is actually verifiable if you're a little clever about it. You can have models grade other models. You can have rubrics. You can set up environments where the feedback is noisy but still informative. The history here is that every time someone says "you can't get a signal for X," someone finds a way to get a weak signal for X, and weak signals turn out to be enough at scale.

But here's where I'd give the other side its due. There's a version of the world where the models become superhuman at everything with a crisp answer and remain stubbornly mediocre at taste, judgment, long-horizon planning in messy environments. And in that world you get something that looks really impressive on benchmarks and is less transformative than it looks. I don't think that's the most likely outcome, but if you asked me what the main way the "country of geniuses in a datacenter" timeline slips, this is probably it. Not that the models hit a wall, but that the wall is lopsided.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that even the lopsided world is a big deal. If you only got superhuman math, code, and the kind of science where the loop closes fast, that's still an enormous fraction of what drives economic and technological progress. So I think of this less as "does the whole thing work or not" and more as "how uneven is the frontier." My bet is less uneven than the skeptics think, but I hold that at something like seventy or eighty percent, not ninety-nine.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the outcome in terms of how uneven the capability frontier is, gives a probabilistic estimate, and says even partial transfer would matter—treating generalization as a matter of degree rather than all-or-nothing.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real possibility. The question is how much of what you learn from verifiable tasks transfers to things that are harder to verify. Coding and math aren’t isolated skills. They involve planning, forming abstractions, noticing when you’ve made a mistake, and trying a different approach. Those abilities should be useful elsewhere. But that doesn’t establish that the transfer will be sufficient.

You could imagine a model that’s extraordinarily good at solving a precisely specified problem, but much less good at deciding which problem to solve. In science, checking a prediction is one part of the process. Coming up with a useful hypothesis, or choosing an experiment that reveals something interesting, is another. We shouldn’t assume that improving the first automatically gives you the second.

At the same time, “verifiable” isn’t necessarily a fixed boundary. Some things are hard to evaluate because the feedback takes a long time, or because you need to interact with the world. If you can build environments that provide that feedback, the range of tasks you can train on expands.

So I’d treat this as an empirical question. As you train more on tasks with clear feedback, do you see improvements on tasks where that feedback is absent? How broad are those improvements, and do they keep going? I expect meaningful transfer, but the possibility that it becomes much weaker outside those domains is something you have to take seriously.

r001.rationale: The response describes transfer as varying in amount and breadth, asking how much it extends and noting it may weaken outside verifiable domains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real possibility. The question is how much of what we call general intelligence you can learn through tasks where you can check the answer. Math and coding are especially convenient because you can generate an answer, test it, and get a fairly clear signal about whether you did well. A lot of the things we ultimately care about don’t have that property, at least in such a straightforward way.

But I wouldn’t equate the scope of the training signal with the scope of the capabilities you acquire. To solve a difficult coding problem, you may have to learn to plan, form hypotheses, notice when an approach isn’t working, and try something else. Those abilities could transfer to domains where the final answer is harder to verify. The empirical question is how much they transfer.

You could imagine a world where we get extraordinarily good mathematicians and programmers, but they’re still missing something important about scientific judgment or dealing with people. You could also imagine that verifiable tasks provide enough of a foundation that relatively modest amounts of training in those other domains unlock much broader abilities. I don’t think we should assume either outcome. We should look at whether progress is showing up on tasks that are meaningfully different from the ones supplying the reward.

r001.rationale: It frames transfer as a question of “how much” learned abilities carry over and presents outcomes ranging from limited transfer to broader capabilities.
